summary.text: A finite case analysis shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\) one can choose primes \(p,q\) with different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and \(\gcd(d,pq)=1\). Thus for any starting value there is an \(i<pq\) with \(a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}\), so one of the first 150 terms has prime divisors \(p\) and \(q\) with different final digits.

full_proof.text:
Let a positive integer be called lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that no arithmetic progression
\[
 a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
with \(a\ge 2\) and \(1\le d\le 2025\) can consist entirely of lopsided numbers. This is the negation of the conjecture.

We first establish the small-prime lemma that supplies the obstruction.

**Small-prime lemma.** For every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le 2025\), there are primes \(p,q\) such that

1. \(p\nmid d\) and \(q\nmid d\);
2. \(p\) and \(q\) have different final decimal digits; and
3. \(pq\le 150\).

To prove this, consider the seven primes
\[
P=\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17\}
\]
and the following list of admissible pairs:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(3,5),(3,7),\\
&(2,11),(2,13),(3,11),(5,7),(3,17),\\
&(5,11),(5,13),(7,11),(7,13),(11,13).
\end{aligned}
\]
Every displayed pair consists of primes having different final digits. Their products, in the same order, are
\[
6,10,14,15,21,22,26,33,35,51,55,65,77,91,143,
\]
so every product is at most \(150\).

Suppose, toward proving the lemma by contradiction, that none of these pairs consists of two primes both failing to divide \(d\). Let
\[
S=\{r\in P:r\nmid d\}.
\]
Thus \(S\) contains no displayed pair. We now classify all possibilities for such a set \(S\), or more precisely all maximal sets with that property.

If \(3\in S\), then none of
\[
2,5,7,11,17
\]
can belong to \(S\), because \((3,2),(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,17)\) all occur in the displayed list. The only other prime from \(P\) that can accompany \(3\) is \(13\). Hence in this case
\[
S\subseteq\{3,13\}.
\]

Now suppose \(3\notin S\). Since \(17\) is paired in the displayed list only with \(3\), adjoining \(17\) to \(S\) cannot create a displayed pair. Thus any maximal set of this kind contains \(17\). Among the remaining primes
\[
2,5,7,11,13,
\]
every pair appears in the displayed list: explicitly, \(2\) is paired with each of \(5,7,11,13\); \(5\) is paired with each of \(7,11,13\); \(7\) is paired with \(11,13\); and \(11\) is paired with \(13\). Therefore at most one of those five primes can accompany \(17\).

Consequently every set \(S\) containing no displayed pair is contained in one of the following six maximal sets:
\[
\{2,17\},\quad \{3,13\},\quad \{5,17\},\quad
\{7,17\},\quad \{11,17\},\quad \{13,17\}.
\]
For each possibility, all primes in the complement in \(P\) divide \(d\). Since those primes are distinct, their product divides \(d\). The six corresponding forced divisors are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{set containing }S& P\setminus S&\text{product of the complement}\\ \hline
\{2,17\}&\{3,5,7,11,13\}&15015\\
\{3,13\}&\{2,5,7,11,17\}&13090\\
\{5,17\}&\{2,3,7,11,13\}&6006\\
\{7,17\}&\{2,3,5,11,13\}&4290\\
\{11,17\}&\{2,3,5,7,13\}&2730\\
\{13,17\}&\{2,3,5,7,11\}&2310.
\end{array}
\]
For example, if \(S\subseteq\{13,17\}\), then \(2,3,5,7,11\) all divide \(d\), so their product \(2310\) divides \(d\). The same reasoning applies in every row. Every product in the last column is greater than \(2025\). Since \(d\) is positive, a positive divisor of \(d\) cannot exceed \(d\); thus each row contradicts \(d\le2025\).

It follows that our supposition was false. Hence at least one displayed pair \((p,q)\) has both \(p\nmid d\) and \(q\nmid d\). As already checked, its primes have different final digits and its product is at most \(150\). This proves the small-prime lemma.

We now apply the lemma to an arbitrary proposed progression. Assume that
\[
a\ge2,\qquad 1\le d\le2025.
\]
Choose \(p,q\) as in the lemma, and put
\[
m=pq.
\]
Because \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,m)=1.
\]
Indeed, every prime divisor of \(pq\) is either \(p\) or \(q\), and neither of these divides \(d\).

Since \(d\) is relatively prime to \(m\), it has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(m\). Let \(u\) satisfy
\[
ud\equiv1\pmod m.
\]
Choose \(i\) to be the unique representative in the range
\[
0\le i<m
\]
of the residue class
\[
i\equiv-au\pmod m.
\]
Multiplying this congruence by \(d\), and using \(ud\equiv1\pmod m\), gives
\[
id\equiv-aud\equiv-a\pmod m.
\]
Therefore
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod m.
\]
Thus \(m=pq\) divides \(a+id\), and in particular
\[
p\mid a+id\qquad\text{and}\qquad q\mid a+id.
\]

Furthermore, the choice of pair gives \(m=pq\le150\). Since \(0\le i<m\), we have
\[
0\le i<150.
\]
Thus \(a+id\) is one of the specified 150 terms of the progression. Also \(a+id\ge a\ge2\), so it is a positive integer greater than \(1\). The primes \(p\) and \(q\) are both prime divisors of this term, but by construction their residues modulo \(10\), and hence their final decimal digits, are different. Consequently the prime divisors of \(a+id\) do not all have the same final decimal digit. Therefore \(a+id\) is not lopsided.

We have shown that for every \(a\ge2\) and every \(d\) with \(1\le d\le2025\), at least one of the terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), fails the defining condition for A381159. Hence there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all 150 terms occur among the numbers whose prime divisors share the same final decimal digit. This disproves the conjecture.
